di.iiii · raw lane · visual audit · 18 aug 2026

A window and a card
are the same rectangle.

You noticed the floating windows look like the nodes. They don't just look alike — they are drawn with the same line, the same fill and the same corner, and neither one casts a shadow. Nothing in the picture says which one is lying on the canvas and which one is floating above it.

Here is the measurement, what it costs us, and six ways out — rendered in the running app so you can pick by eye.

The measurement

One costume, two different animals

I measured both objects in the live editor rather than reading the stylesheet, so these are the numbers the browser actually paints. Red means the two objects are identical on that property.

PropertyNode cardFloating window
Border1px solid rgba(77,249,255,.3)1px solid rgba(77,249,255,.3)identical
Corner radius00identical
Shadownonenoneidentical
Fill#000000#0a0a0a1.6% apart
Header height44px66pxdiffers
Name typographyInter 700 · 12pxInter 700 · 18.72pxdiffers
Kind label"numbers" — the family, in the family's colour"VIEW.TEXT" — the internal type id, greytwo vocabularies
Controlsone 13px chevronfour bordered buttons, each repeating the frame's own borderdiffers

The window's name is not a design decision at all. Its stylesheet sets exactly one property on the title — a zero margin — so the size and weight you see are the browser's built-in heading style. That is why the window shouts and the card whispers: one was authored, the other was left to Chrome.

the same line, everywhere

On one screen of the editor, 23 separate elements are drawn with that identical cyan hairline: the cards, the windows, every window button, the palette, the zoom cluster, the topbar buttons. 326 elements have square corners. 0 elements cast any shadow at all. In the stylesheet, 67 rules declare that one border and only 6 mention a shadow.

What it costs

Four things the picture cannot say

↕

Depth is invisible

A window sitting on top of three cards simply clips them, with no shadow, no dimming and no edge change. The eye reads one flat collage instead of "this is in front". Bring a second window up and nothing tells you which has focus — there is no focused state anywhere in the stylesheet.

⇄

The two identity systems are swapped

Both objects use the same grammar — a small mono label plus a big bold name — but the card puts the small label on the right and the window puts it on top. Worse, they say different things: the card learned to speak plainly last week ("the room", "make", "watch", in each family's colour) while the window still shows the code's internal name, UNIVERSE.WORLD. The vocabulary fix landed on half the product.

▣

Every control repeats the frame

The four buttons in a window header carry exactly the frame's own border, so a window reads as a rectangle containing four smaller rectangles — the strongest single reason it looks like a card with cards inside it. And they are all equal weight: Close looks exactly like Pin.

›

The one thing that IS the same is styled differently

Stepping into a node — the move at the heart of joining Raw and Studio — is a bare 13px chevron on a card and a full labelled button in a window. The genuinely shared action looks unrelated; the genuinely different objects look identical. It is exactly backwards.

Found along the way

Six things that are simply broken

None of these are style opinions. They are defects the audit turned up, worth fixing whichever direction you choose.

WhatWhere
Window buttons are 37px tall — under the 44px one-finger floor this project holds every other control to, and stated as a rule in a comment two hundred lines away in the same file. .raw-window-actions button
The way into a node is a 32px target on a phone — the chevron is the only path in on touch, and it is smaller than the floor too. .raw-graph-node-enter-hint
Window buttons render in Arial. No font is declared, so they fall back to the browser default while every other word in the product is Inter. .raw-window-actions button
Pinning a window has no visible effect. The markup applies is-pinned and is-minimized; the stylesheet has no rule for either. A pinned window is indistinguishable from an unpinned one. DesktopWindow.jsx
A card style points at a colour that does not exist. --di-card is used once and defined nowhere, so that background silently never applies. raw.css:751
No window chrome adapts to a phone. Of fourteen responsive rules in the file, not one touches the window frame, header, buttons or the 16px resize corner. raw.css @media

While we were in there

The stylesheet is carrying luggage

Raw's look lives in one 4,246-line file, and a real share of it dresses things that no longer exist. I checked each of these by searching every component for the name — nothing renders them:

Dead dialectWhat it was
.raw-op-create-*An entire node-creation dialog — about 120 lines. Its component was deleted in July 2026, and the later rename from Seed to Raw dutifully renamed the orphaned styles without noticing.
.raw-system-window-*A second, unfinished window chrome — and the only container in the file with a white edge instead of a cyan one.
.raw-world-type-*, .raw-world-node-*An older in-world card language, replaced by the graph cards.
.raw-view-*, .raw-root-canvas-*Two earlier attempts at the canvas surface.
Plus the assets and activity panels: the layout registers window sizes for them, but no code ever draws them, so both would open as a plain text box. Their styling can never be reached.

And the discipline has slipped in a way that guarantees drift: the project defines a font token for its label typeface, and the file uses that token once — while typing the same font stack out by hand 43 times. Square corners appear 41 times, but four other corner sizes have crept in for what are all the same kind of small boxed field. Four labels are styled to look like the mono system labels but are silently set in Inter, because no font was declared on them.

Six looks, rendered

What we can do

Each of these is the real editor with styling injected into the running page — nothing in the repo has changed. Same desk every time: the World window in front, three cards behind it. Verdicts are mine, from looking at all six.

A · Today

baseline

The window covers three cards and the only sign is that they stop. Its edge is the same hairline as theirs.

This is what you were reacting to.

B · Add a shadow

doesn't work

The obvious fix, and it fails: a black shadow on a black canvas is invisible. Compare it with A and you will struggle to see any difference — I did.

Worth knowing, because it rules out the standard answer. On this palette depth has to come from hue and fill, not shade.

Cost: three lines. Effect: none.

C · Author the header

smallest real fix

Frame untouched — still square, still cyan. Only the header changes: the name drops to a deliberate 13px, the kind label speaks the plain vocabulary in its family's colour, and the four buttons become quiet text that lights up on hover.

The "card full of little cards" effect disappears. The window still belongs to the same visual family as the cards, which may be exactly what you want.

Cost: one CSS block, no structural change.

D · Join the documented panel family

most consistent

The repo already has a written rule for floating panels — translucent near-black, a 16px blur, a soft white edge, 6px corners — and Studio's own panels follow it. Raw's windows never did. This makes them match.

It reads beautifully and it ends a real divergence. The price is the square corner: Raw stops being flat and brutal and starts being glassy.

Cost: one CSS block. Changes the lane's character.

E · Lift the fill, keep the cyan

subtle

Square and cyan stay. The window's fill is raised from black to a lit charcoal with a one-pixel highlight along its top edge — the way depth is faked on dark screens where shadows can't be seen.

It works, but quietly: the window still reads as the same species, only brighter.

Cost: one CSS block. Preserves the look completely.

F · Give the cyan back to the graph

half of the answer

Corners stay square — nothing gets glassy. The one change is whose colour the edge is: cyan stops being the border of everything and becomes the mark of the graph (cards, ports, wires), while a window takes a neutral edge over a lifted fill.

Look at it next to A. The cards are unmistakably the canvas; the window is unmistakably in front of it. And you can now tell a window from a card at a glance on a phone, where everything is stacked.

Cost: one CSS block, plus the six defects above. No card changes, no structural work, no new visual language invented.

The one worth doing

G · One job per colour

All six above are reskins of a window frame. This is the only one that treats the actual disease, which is not "the window looks like a card" — it is that cyan is the border of everything, so it means nothing. Give each colour exactly one job and the confusion cannot come back:

▭

Neutral is furniture

Windows, the palette, the topbar, the zoom cluster — everything that is not the work itself takes a plain white-alpha edge over a lifted fill. Furniture should be quiet.

◆

Family hue is what a thing is

A card's edge and icon take its family colour, instead of naming it in a 10px word nobody reads at arm's length. A window hosting that node carries the same hue as a stripe along its top edge — so a window and its card are visibly one thing, which is exactly what joining Raw and Studio has to communicate.

✳

Cyan is interaction, nothing else

Selected, hovered, focused. It stops being decoration and becomes information — and because it is suddenly rare, it reads instantly.

◦

Port colour stays data type

Untouched. The wires already speak this language correctly.

the one decision this forces

Our "make" family is #8be9fd — almost the accent cyan. In the phone shot above, the welcome window's stripe reads as chrome rather than as a family. If cyan is to mean interaction, "make" has to move off it. That is a five-minute palette decision, and the only thing in this plan I cannot settle without you.

Before we touch anything

The repo argues with itself here

Two of our own documents give opposite instructions about this exact question. Whichever way you go, one of them needs updating in the same change — otherwise the next agent undoes it.

says change it The single source of truth for every visual decision… The goal is a single visual family across every surface. docs/ai/ui-system.md — and it lists square corners as a drift symptom to fix on sight
says leave it …deliberately leaves colour, type and spacing alone, because the visual language is locked and consolidating it invites drift. docs/raw/LAYOUT_CANVAS_FIRST.md — the Raw layout proposal

My reading: the second one is protecting against a sweeping re-colour of the whole lane, which is not what this is. Changing one object's edge so the lane's own accent means something again is the opposite of drift. But it is your call, and it is a real disagreement rather than an oversight.

If you say go

What I would ship, in order

  1. The six defects, on their own — touch targets, the Arial buttons, the pinned state that shows nothing, the colour that does not exist. No look changes, so nothing to argue about.
  2. The window header authored: real 13px name, the plain family vocabulary instead of UNIVERSE.WORLD, quiet controls, Close set apart. This is most of the improvement, and it is reversible in one commit.
  3. Chrome goes neutral — windows first, then the palette, topbar and zoom cluster, so the rule holds everywhere rather than in one place.
  4. The family hue moves from a word to the card's own edge and icon, and onto its window as a top stripe. Cyan is then cut back to selection, hover and focus only — which also finally gives the front window a focused state.
  5. Move "make" off cyan in the family palette, so the two systems stop colliding.
  6. Whichever of the two documents you overruled gets corrected in the same change, and the wiki entry that describes windows gets the new picture.
  7. Separately, and safe to do any time: delete the dead dialects and put the label font behind its token. That is a smaller file and one less way for the next person to drift.

Cards themselves I would not touch. They are doing their job, and the families work that just landed made them clearer, not muddier — the windows are simply the half that got left behind.

Measured in the running editor at 1440×900 and 390×844 (device pixel ratio 3), branch dev, 18 August 2026.
Variants B–F are CSS injected into the live page for photographing. Nothing in the repository was changed to make this audit.
